title: Celsus traces the saying on worldly wisdom to the Greeks
source_text: Διὸ μεταβαίνομεν ἐπ᾿ ἄλλην Κέλσου κατηγορίαν. οὐδὲ τὰς λέξεις ἡμῶν εἰδότος ἀλλ᾿ ἐκ παρακουσματίων φήσαντος ὅτι φαμὲν τὴν ἐν ἀνθρώποις σοφίαν μωρίαν εἶναι παρὰ θεῷ, τοῦ Παύλου λέγοντος· „ἡ σοφία τοῦ κόσμου μωρία παρὰ θεῷ ἐστι.“ καί φησιν ὁ Κέλσος ὅτι ἡ τούτου αἰτία καὶ πάλαι εἴρηται. οἴεται δὲ αἰτίαν εἶναι τὸ βούλεσθαι ἡμᾶς διὰ τῆς λέξεως ταύτης τοὺς ἀπαιδεύτους καὶ ἠλιθίους προσάγεσθαι μόνους. ἀλλ᾿ ὡς καὶ αὐτὸς ἐσημειώσατο, ταὐτὸ εἶπεν ἀνωτέρω, καὶ ἡμεῖς πρὸς τὸν λόγον κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἡμῖν ἀπηντήσαμεν. ὅμως μέντοι ἐβουλήθη καὶ τοῦτο δεῖξαι πεπλασμένον ἡμῖν καὶ ληφθὲν ἀπὸ τῶν παρ᾿ Ἕλλησι σοφῶν. ἄλλην μὲν εἶναι φησάντων τὴν ἀνθρωπίνην σοφίαν ἄλλην δὲ τὴν θείαν. καὶ ἐκτίθεταί γε Ἡρακλείτου λέξεις, μίαν μὲν, ἐν ᾗ φησιν· „ἦθος γὰρ ἀνθρώπειον μὲν οὐκ ἔχει γνώμας, θεῖον δὲ ἔχει,“ ἑτέραν δέ· „ἀνὴρ νήπιος ἤκουσε πρὸς δαίμονος ὅκως περ παῖς πρὸς ἀνδρός.“ ἐκτίθεται δὲ καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς Πλάτωνος γεγραμμένης Σωκράτους ἀπολογίας ταῦτα· „ἐγὼ γὰρ, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, δι᾿ οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἢ διὰ σοφίαν τοῦτο τὸ ὄνομα ἔσχηκα. ποίαν δὲ σοφίαν ταύτην; ἥπερ ἐστὶν ἴσως ἀνθρωπίνη σοφία· τῷ ὄντι γὰρ κινδυνεύω ταύτην εἶναι σοφός.“ ἃ μὲν οὖν ἐκτίθεται ὁ Κέλσος ταῦτά ἐστιν. ἐγὼ δὲ ἀπὸ τῆς πρὸς Ἑρμείαν καὶ Ἔραστον καὶ Κορίσκον Πλάτωνος ἐπιστολῆς καὶ ταῦτα παραθήσομαι· „Ἐράστῳ δὲ καὶ Κορίσκῳ πρὸς τῇ τῶν εἰδῶν σοφίᾳ τῇ καλῇ ταύτῃ φημὶ ἐγὼ καίπερ γέρων ὢν προσδεῖν σοφίας τῆς περὶ τοὺς πονηροὺς καὶ ἀδίκους φυλακτικῆς καί τινος ἀμυντικῆς δυνάμεως. ἄπειροι γάρ εἰσι διὰ τὸ μεθ᾿ ἡμῶν μετρίων ὄντων καὶ οὐ κακῶν συχνὸν διατετριφέναι τοῦ βίου· διὸ δὴ τούτων προσδεῖν εἶπον, ἵνα μὴ ἀναγκάζωνται τῆς ἀληθινῆς μὲν ἀμελεῖν σοφίας, τῆς δ᾿ ἀνθρωπίνης τε καὶ ἀναγκαίας ἐπιμελεῖσθαι μειζόνως ἢ δεῖ.“
pass_a_gloss: Therefore we pass over (μεταβαίνομεν) to another accusation (κατηγορία) of Celsus, [he] not even knowing our words (λέξεις) but from mishearings (παρακουσμάτια) having said that we say the wisdom among men (ἡ ἐν ἀνθρώποις σοφία) is foolishness (μωρία) with God (παρὰ θεῷ), Paul saying [gen. abs.]: 'the wisdom of the world (κόσμος) is foolishness with God.' And Celsus says that the cause (αἰτία) of this has also been said long since/earlier (πάλαι εἴρηται). He thinks (οἴεται) the cause is our wishing through this saying (λέξις) to draw to ourselves (προσάγεσθαι) only the uneducated (ἀπαίδευτοι) and stupid (ἠλίθιοι). But as he himself noted (ἐσημειώσατο), he said the same thing above (ἀνωτέρω), and we met (ἀπηντήσαμεν) the argument as far as was possible for us. Nevertheless he wished to show this too as fabricated (πεπλασμένον) by us and taken (ληφθέν) from the wise among the Greeks, who said human (ἀνθρωπίνη) wisdom is one and divine (θεία) another. And he sets out (ἐκτίθεται) words of Heraclitus, one in which he says: 'for human character (ἦθος ἀνθρώπειον) does not have judgments/insights (γνῶμαι), but divine has'; another: 'a man is called (ἤκουσε, 'is spoken of as') an infant (νήπιος) by a daimon (δαίμων), just as a child by a man.' He sets out also from Plato's written Apology of Socrates these: 'For I, men of Athens, through nothing other than through wisdom have got (ἔσχηκα) this name (ὄνομα). What wisdom is this? That which is perhaps human wisdom; for in reality (τῷ ὄντι) I run the risk (κινδυνεύω) of being wise in this.' What Celsus sets out, then, is these. But I from Plato's letter (ἐπιστολή) to Hermias and Erastus and Coriscus will set beside (παραθήσομαι) these also: 'To Erastus and Coriscus, besides (πρός) this fine wisdom of the forms (εἴδη), I say, although being old (γέρων), there is further need (προσδεῖν) of a wisdom guarding (φυλακτική) concerning the wicked (πονηροί) and unjust (ἄδικοι) and of some defensive power (ἀμυντικὴ δύναμις). For they are inexperienced (ἄπειροι) through having spent much of life with us, being moderate (μέτριοι) and not bad (κακοί); therefore I said they need these in addition, so that they may not be compelled (ἀναγκάζωνται) to neglect (ἀμελεῖν) the true (ἀληθινή) wisdom, and to care for (ἐπιμελεῖσθαι) the human and necessary (ἀναγκαία) more greatly than is needful (ἢ δεῖ).'
pass_b_english: So we pass on to another charge of Celsus. He does not even know our actual words, but from scraps he has misheard he said that we say “the wisdom among men is foolishness with God,” although what Paul says is: “The wisdom of the world is foolishness with God” (1 Corinthians 3:19). Celsus says that the reason for this has been given already. He thinks the reason is that by this saying we want to win over only the uneducated and the stupid. But, as he himself noted, he said the same thing earlier, and we have answered that argument as well as we could. Even so, he wanted to show that this too was made up by us and taken from the wise men of the Greeks, who said that human wisdom is one thing and divine wisdom another.

He does indeed set out sayings of Heraclitus: one in which he says, “For human character has no insight, but divine character has” (Heraclitus, fragment 78 DK), and another, “A man is called an infant by a divinity, as a child is by a man” (Heraclitus, fragment 79 DK). He also sets out these words from the Apology of Socrates written by Plato: “For I, men of Athens, have gained this name through nothing else than wisdom. What sort of wisdom is this? The kind that is perhaps human wisdom; for in truth I may well be wise in that” (Plato, Apology 20d).

These, then, are the passages Celsus sets out. I will add these as well, from Plato’s letter to Hermias, Erastus and Coriscus: “To Erastus and Coriscus I say, old as I am, that besides this fine wisdom of the Forms they still need a wisdom that guards against wicked and unjust men, and a certain power of self-defence. For they lack experience, because they have spent much of their life with us, who are moderate men and not bad ones. That is why I said they still need these things, so that they may not be forced to neglect the true wisdom and to attend to the human and necessary kind more than they should” (Plato, Letter 6, 322d–e).

choices.choice: Origen’s point in the first sentence is that Celsus misquotes: Celsus has ‘the wisdom among men’, Paul has ‘the wisdom of the world’ (1 Corinthians 3:19); ‘of the world’ keeps Paul’s κόσμου without adding ‘this’. Celsus’s claim that ‘the reason has been given already’ is indirect speech in the Greek and is kept indirect; πάλαι refers to Celsus’s own earlier statement, and Origen’s earlier reply is probably the discussion in Book 1 and Book 3 (not cited inline because the exact place is not stated). The Heraclitus sayings are Diels-Kranz 22 B 78 and B 79, both preserved by this passage; ἤκουσε is the idiom ‘is spoken of as’. The Apology quotation (20d) lacks Plato’s τινα (‘a certain wisdom’); translated as Origen gives it. The letter is Plato’s Sixth Letter (322d–e); Hermias is named in the address but not in the quoted lines. These classical quotations are set in double quotation marks as quoted texts; they are not Celsus’s own words.

'He sets out, indeed, some sayings' smoothed to 'He does indeed set out sayings' (καὶ ἐκτίθεταί γε)
